newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian truckers reach accord to end 10-day strike.
newsitem.headline: Indian truckers reach accord to end 10-day strike.

text.p: India's truck owners agreed on Wednesday to end a 10-day strike that hit the economy and pushed up prices following an accord to bring back 2.2 million vehicles on the roads, a senior government official said.
"The strike is over," said the Surface Transport Ministry official, who said the accord was reached just 15 minutes after talks broke down.
"They agreed. We agreed. That's all," said the official.
The truckers had launched the strike to protest against a five percent service tax and a hike in insurance premiums proposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget.
The official said the government had agreed that a Tariff Advisory Committee would look into the truckers' complaints about high insurance premiums.
Other details were not immediately available. Truck owners could not be reached for comment.

S.P.Singh, spokesman for the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), the truckers' union, told Reuters earlier on Wednesday that the strike would continue, reversing an earlier statement that the truckers were on the verge of an agreement.

Hours before that, Singh had said the government had agreed to the truck-owners shedding their responsibility to collect the service tax and also agreed to keep a hike in insurance premiums in abeyance.
Singh said later that the talks broke down after AIMTC officials met government officials. He did not give reasons.
AIMTC secretary-general Chittranjan Dass said on Tuesday that the government and the truck owners had reached a draft agreement which fell short of the demand to remove the service tax.

The centre-left coalition of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, fighting for its life after the Congress party withdrew its support, has said it cannot rescind the tax because the budget proposals are before parliament and yet to be approved.
The budget is being held hostage by the political crisis. Deve Gowda faces a confidence vote on Friday.
"If the budget is not passed, then the whole problem would be solved," Singh said. "But still we have to wait and watch."
Yogendra Narain, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, said the transport of essential commodities had been satisfactory in most states.
"Prices have certainly not risen substantially," he said. "But the strike has definitely affected industry and ports."
S.V. Damankar, secretary of the Bombay Port Trust, which is among India's busiest ports, said cargo handling had fallen off to 3,000 tonnes a day compared with the usual 250,000 tonnes.
Analysts said businesses that depended on agricultural produce were the worst-hit as movements had been restricted.
"The economy is losing at least 70 billion to 80 billion rupees ($1.9 billion to $2.2 billion) per day," K.R. Vishwanathan, a senior economist at the Birla Economic Research Foundation, told Reuters.
